doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Looking back: preparation, security and dance band roots
summary: Feeling comfort for the first time, advice to be prepared, and film czars from dance bands.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Yeah. Don’t fly it, okay. Keep it on the ground. Is there something in your career that you haven’t done yet that you’d like to?

It’s funny, that’s a very good question because sometimes Ruth and I talk about that, if there’s — you know sometimes you get so involved in what you do for a living that you forget everything else. And I really can honestly say, because I’ve always been a nervous wreck all my life. Tomorrow is Armageddon. Because this is that kind of a business. I mean we used to say at NBC there’s a twelve year old walking behind you, he wants your job. I’m serious. And I think I’ve always lived in that factory of insecurity. And I think for the first time, because I have a wonderful orchestra at Carnegie Hall, and I get to guest conduct some wonderful orchestras, and I think for the first time I have almost, I should never say it, but I almost have a comfort. And I think it’s too late for me to try anything else. I’m so bloody lucky that I’ve stumbled through all these transitions of music, I mean starting with territory bands or starting in a roadhouse, and being able to

climb a very long hill. And I was never a very good politician. You know everybody talks about, oh politics, everything is politics. I don’t believe that’s true. I think it’s association, friendship, and as Crosby used to say, be prepared. And that’s what I feel. If you get a chance to make a step of any kind, be prepared. You know what you’re doing before you get there. And the guys that I watched in the early days of music at Metro, the czars, I mean they didn’t make a statement if they didn’t know what they were saying.
Some of the major czars as you say, were actually pretty hip musically, weren’t they? In the early days?

Oh surely. Well a lot of them came from, some of them like Johnny Green they came from dance band experience. A lot of them did. A lot of the orchestrators. Where are you going to learn to write like that? You start with the dance band, like the great American composer William Schuman, began his life writing for dance bands. I couldn’t believe that. He told me he had a dance band in New York, for years he said, that’s why he said he was so glad to get away from saxophones. And I to this day am not a saxophone man either, except Newsom.
Yeah. Tommy Newsom. He could play anything anytime for me. He’s so wonderful.
